title: Organic Chemistry: Foundations
description: The chemistry of carbon compounds: how they are built, named, shaped and made to react.

entries.name: Functional groups
entries.tagline: The reactive parts of organic molecules, which decide how they behave.

sections.text: A functional group is an atom or small group of atoms in a molecule that gives it characteristic reactions. Molecules with the same functional group react in similar ways, whatever the rest of the molecule is.

facts: C–C and C–H single bonds only. Methane, CH₄.
C–X, with X = F, Cl, Br or I. Chloromethane, CH₃Cl.
–CHO, a carbonyl at the end of a chain. Ethanal, CH₃CHO.
C=O in the middle of a chain. Propanone (acetone), CH₃COCH₃.

sections.text: To predict a reaction, find the functional groups first. Infrared spectroscopy and NMR are used to identify them.

quiz.q: What is the functional group of an alcohol?

entries.name: Alkanes and IUPAC naming
entries.tagline: The simplest organic compounds, and the rules for naming any of them.

sections.text: Alkanes contain only carbon and hydrogen with single bonds. Open-chain alkanes have the formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, and cycloalkanes CₙH₂ₙ. They burn well but are otherwise rather unreactive.
1 meth, 2 eth, 3 prop, 4 but, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 hept, 8 oct, 9 non, 10 dec, each followed by -ane for an alkane.

points: Find the longest continuous carbon chain. That gives the parent name.
Number the chain from the end that gives the first branch the lower number.
Name each branch (substituent) as methyl, ethyl, chloro and so on, and give its position number.
List the branches alphabetically. Use di-, tri- for repeats (these prefixes are ignored when alphabetizing).
CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is 2-methylbutane.
A six-carbon ring is cyclohexane.

quiz.q: What is the formula of an open-chain alkane with n carbon atoms?

entries.name: Isomerism
entries.tagline: Different molecules with the same molecular formula.

facts: Same formula, atoms joined in a different order. Butane and 2-methylpropane are both C₄H₁₀. Ethanol and dimethyl ether are both C₂H₆O, but one is an alcohol and the other is an ether.
Same atoms joined in the same order, but arranged differently in space.

points: Cis–trans (geometric) isomers: found in alkenes and rings, where rotation is restricted. Cis has the two similar groups on the same side and trans on opposite sides. Cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene have different melting and boiling points.
Enantiomers and diastereomers, which arise from chirality (see Chirality and enantiomers).

sections.text: Isomers can have very different properties. Ethanol is a drinkable alcohol, and its isomer dimethyl ether is a gas used as a propellant.

quiz.q: Ethanol and dimethyl ether (both C₂H₆O) are examples of…

entries.name: Chirality and enantiomers
entries.tagline: Molecules that are mirror images but cannot be placed on top of each other, like left and right hands.

sections.text: A carbon with four different groups attached is a chiral center (stereocenter). A molecule with one chiral center exists as two forms that are non-superimposable mirror images. These are enantiomers.

points: Enantiomers have identical melting points, boiling points and reactions with achiral reagents.
They rotate plane-polarized light by equal amounts in opposite directions. This is called optical activity.
A 50:50 mixture is a racemic mixture, which does not rotate light.
In the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog system, each center is labeled R or S.

sections.text: A molecule with n stereocenters can have up to 2ⁿ stereoisomers. Stereoisomers that are not mirror images are called diastereomers, and they have different physical properties. A meso compound has stereocenters but is achiral because of an internal mirror plane, as in meso-tartaric acid.

Living things are chiral, so enantiomers often act differently. One form of limonene smells of oranges and the other of lemons. The two forms of a drug can have very different effects in the body, and thalidomide is the cautionary example.

quiz.a: A carbon bonded to four different groups
wrong: A carbon with a double bond

entries.name: Conformations and cyclohexane
entries.tagline: The shapes a molecule takes as its single bonds rotate.

sections.text: Atoms can rotate around a single bond, so one molecule has many shapes called conformations. They are not different compounds, and they interconvert quickly at room temperature.

points: A Newman projection looks down a C–C bond. In the staggered conformation the groups on the two carbons are as far apart as possible, and in the eclipsed one they line up.
Staggered is lower in energy than eclipsed. For ethane the difference is about 12 kJ/mol.
In butane, the anti conformation (the two methyl groups opposite) is the most stable. The gauche conformation is about 3.8 kJ/mol higher.
The ring is not flat. It takes a chair shape with all bond angles close to 109.5°, which is almost free of strain.
Each carbon has one axial position (pointing up or down) and one equatorial position (pointing outward).
A ring flip swaps axial and equatorial. Bulky groups prefer to be equatorial, where they have more room.
At room temperature, methylcyclohexane has about 95% of its molecules with the methyl group equatorial.

quiz.q: Which position do bulky groups prefer on a cyclohexane chair?

entries.name: Mechanisms, curved arrows and carbocations
entries.tagline: How chemists draw the movement of electrons in a reaction.

sections.text: A reaction mechanism shows, step by step, how bonds break and form. Curved arrows show the movement of electron pairs: the tail starts at the electrons (a bond or a lone pair) and the head points to where they go. A half-headed arrow shows the movement of one electron.

points: Heterolytic: both bonding electrons go to one atom, giving ions.
Homolytic: one electron goes to each atom, giving two radicals.

sections.text: A carbocation is a carbon with three bonds and a positive charge. Its stability goes tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl, because alkyl groups donate electron density (inductive effect and hyperconjugation). This is why SN1 and E1 reactions prefer tertiary substrates, and why Markovnikov addition happens.
Chlorination of methane with light shows the three stages:
points: Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl· (light breaks the Cl–Cl bond).
Propagation: Cl· + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃·, then CH₃· + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl·. The chain keeps going.
Termination: two radicals combine, such as Cl· + Cl· → Cl₂.

quiz.q: Which carbocation is the most stable?

entries.name: Nucleophilic substitution: SN1 and SN2
entries.tagline: A nucleophile replaces a leaving group on a carbon.

sections.text: A nucleophile is an electron-rich species that donates a pair of electrons, such as OH⁻, CN⁻ or NH₃. An electrophile is electron-poor and accepts electrons. In substitution, a nucleophile replaces a leaving group on a saturated carbon. Good leaving groups are weak bases: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻, with F⁻ very poor.

facts: One step. The nucleophile attacks from the back as the leaving group departs. Rate = k[RX][Nu], second order. Inverts the stereochemistry. Fastest for methyl and primary carbons, and blocked by bulky groups. Favored by strong nucleophiles and polar aprotic solvents such as acetone or DMSO.

Two steps. The leaving group leaves first to give a carbocation, then the nucleophile attacks. Rate = k[RX], first order. Gives a racemic mixture from a chiral center. Fastest for tertiary carbons. Favored by weak nucleophiles and polar protic solvents such as water and alcohols.

points: Methyl and primary substrates: SN2.
Tertiary substrates: SN1 (SN2 is blocked).
Secondary substrates: depends on the nucleophile and solvent.

quiz.q: Which type of substrate reacts fastest by SN2?
What does an SN2 reaction do to the stereochemistry at the carbon?

entries.name: Elimination: E1 and E2
entries.tagline: Removing a small molecule to make a double bond.

sections.text: In an elimination, a base removes a hydrogen from the carbon next to the carbon bearing the leaving group, and the leaving group leaves. The result is an alkene.

facts: One step. A strong base removes the H as the leaving group leaves, with the H and the leaving group on opposite sides (anti-periplanar). Rate = k[RX][Base].
Two steps, through the same carbocation as SN1. Rate = k[RX]. Favored by tertiary substrates, weak bases and heat.

sections.text: When more than one alkene can form, the more substituted (more stable) alkene is usually the major product. A bulky base, such as potassium tert-butoxide, gives mostly the less substituted alkene instead.

points: Heat favors elimination, since elimination makes more molecules and so gains entropy.
Strong, bulky bases favor elimination. Good nucleophiles that are weak bases favor substitution.
Dehydration of an alcohol with hot concentrated sulfuric acid is an elimination that makes an alkene.

quiz.q: According to Zaitsev's rule, which alkene is usually the major product?
wrong: The one with a triple bond

entries.name: Alkenes, alkynes and addition reactions
entries.tagline: Compounds with double or triple bonds add other molecules across them.

sections.text: A carbon–carbon double bond has one sigma bond and one weaker pi bond. The pi electrons are exposed and attract electrophiles, so alkenes mostly react by addition, in which the pi bond breaks and two new single bonds form.

facts: H₂ with a Pt, Pd or Ni catalyst. Gives an alkane. Used to turn liquid vegetable oils into solid fats.
Br₂ or Cl₂ across the double bond. Bromine water turns from orange to colorless, which is a test for C=C.
HBr or HCl across the double bond. Gives an alkyl halide.
Water with an acid catalyst. Gives an alcohol.

sections.text: In the addition of HX to an unsymmetrical alkene, the H goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogens, and X goes to the other. The reason is that this makes the more stable carbocation. Propene + HBr gives mostly 2-bromopropane.
Alkynes add the same reagents, twice if there is enough. Terminal alkynes are weakly acidic (pKa about 25).

quiz.q: Which test shows a molecule has a C=C double bond?

entries.name: Benzene and aromatic compounds
entries.tagline: A ring with delocalized electrons that is unusually stable.

sections.text: Benzene, C₆H₆, is a flat ring of six carbons. Its six pi electrons are spread evenly around the ring, so all the C–C bonds are the same length (139 pm), between a single and a double bond. The structure is a resonance hybrid, and the extra stability is called aromaticity.
A flat, ring-shaped molecule with a continuous set of p orbitals and 4n + 2 pi electrons (2, 6, 10 …) is aromatic. This is Hückel's rule.
Benzene does not undergo addition, because that would lose the aromatic stability. Instead it does electrophilic aromatic substitution, which swaps an H for an electrophile.
points: Nitration: HNO₃ with H₂SO₄ gives nitrobenzene.
Halogenation: Br₂ with FeBr₃ gives bromobenzene.
Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation: an alkyl or acyl chloride with AlCl₃.
Activating groups that donate electrons (–OH, –NH₂, –CH₃) make the ring react faster and direct new groups to the ortho and para positions.
Deactivating groups that withdraw electrons (–NO₂, –CN, –C=O) make the ring slower and direct to meta. Halogens are deactivating but still direct ortho and para.

quiz.q: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition?
quiz.a: Substitution keeps the stable aromatic ring
wrong: It is not reactive at all

entries.name: Alcohols and ethers
entries.tagline: Compounds with C–O bonds, from drinks to solvents.

sections.text: An alcohol has an –OH group on a saturated carbon. They are classed as primary, secondary or tertiary by how many carbons are attached to the carbon bearing the OH (1, 2 or 3).
points: Hydrogen bonding gives them much higher boiling points than similar ethers. Ethanol boils at 78 °C and its isomer dimethyl ether at −24 °C.
Small alcohols mix with water.
Primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid. A mild reagent such as PCC stops at the aldehyde. Acidified dichromate or permanganate under reflux goes all the way to the acid.
Secondary alcohol → ketone.
Tertiary alcohols do not oxidize, because the carbon has no hydrogen to lose.
Dehydration with hot concentrated sulfuric acid gives an alkene.
With HBr or HCl, an alcohol becomes an alkyl halide, since protonating the OH turns it into a good leaving group (water).

sections.text: R–O–R. Fairly unreactive, so diethyl ether and tetrahydrofuran (THF) are common solvents. Stored ethers slowly form explosive peroxides.

quiz.q: What does a secondary alcohol give when oxidized?

entries.name: Aldehydes and ketones
entries.tagline: The C=O group, whose carbon is attacked by nucleophiles.

sections.text: The C=O bond is polar, with a partly positive carbon and a partly negative oxygen. Nucleophiles attack the carbon, and the pi bond breaks to give an alkoxide, which picks up a proton. This is nucleophilic addition.

facts: Sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) or lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄) adds hydride. Aldehydes give primary alcohols and ketones give secondary alcohols.

RMgX adds R⁻. Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol, other aldehydes give secondary alcohols and ketones give tertiary alcohols. It must be done in dry ether, because Grignard reagents react with water.
Primary amines add to give imines (C=N).
A base removes an alpha hydrogen next to the carbonyl, and the resulting enolate attacks another carbonyl, joining two molecules with a new C–C bond.

sections.text: Aldehydes are easily oxidized and ketones are not. With Tollens' reagent (silver ions in ammonia), an aldehyde gives a silver mirror, and a ketone gives nothing.

quiz.q: What does a Grignard reagent add to a ketone to give?

entries.name: Carboxylic acids and their derivatives
entries.tagline: Acids, esters and amides, and how they interconvert.

sections.text: A carboxylic acid contains –COOH. It is a weak acid (acetic acid has pKa 4.76) but much stronger than an alcohol, because the carboxylate ion is stabilized by resonance.

Acyl chloride > acid anhydride > ester ≈ carboxylic acid > amide. A more reactive derivative can be turned into a less reactive one by a nucleophile replacing the leaving group. This is nucleophilic acyl substitution.

points: Fischer esterification: the equation above, catalyzed by acid. It is an equilibrium, so removing water or using excess alcohol pushes it forward. Esters often smell fruity.
Saponification: an ester heated with NaOH gives the carboxylate salt and the alcohol. Soap is made from fats (esters of glycerol) this way.
Amide formation: an amine with an acyl chloride. Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by amide links called peptide bonds.

quiz.q: What is formed when a fat is heated with sodium hydroxide?

entries.name: Amines
entries.tagline: Organic derivatives of ammonia, basic and nucleophilic.

sections.text: Amines have a nitrogen with a lone pair. They are classed as primary (RNH₂), secondary (R₂NH) or tertiary (R₃N) by how many carbons are on the nitrogen.

points: Basic: the lone pair picks up a proton to give an ammonium ion. The conjugate acids have pKa about 10–11, so amines are stronger bases than most organic compounds, but much weaker than hydroxide.
Nucleophilic: the lone pair attacks electrophiles such as alkyl halides and acyl chlorides.
Aromatic amines such as aniline are weaker bases, because the lone pair is partly delocalized into the ring.
Amides are not basic, because the lone pair is delocalized onto the carbonyl.
Low-mass amines have a fishy smell.

sections.text: Many natural drugs and poisons are amines, called alkaloids, including caffeine, nicotine, morphine and quinine.

quiz.a: The nitrogen has a lone pair that can accept a proton

entries.name: Polymers
entries.tagline: Very long molecules built from many small repeating units.

sections.text: A polymer is a large molecule made of many repeating units called monomers. There are two main ways to make one.
Alkene monomers add to each other, opening the double bond, with nothing lost.
Monomers with two functional groups join, giving off a small molecule, usually water, at each link.
facts: A diamine and a diacid joined by amide links.
A diol and a diacid joined by ester links. Drink bottles and fibers.

points: Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remolded. Thermosets are cross-linked, so they set permanently and char instead of melting.
Chain length, branching and cross-linking control the properties. High-density polyethylene has straight chains and is stiffer than low-density polyethylene, which is branched.

quiz.q: What is released at each link when a condensation polymer forms?
quiz.a: A small molecule such as water
